title: Building Finishing Contractors in the US (2025–2026)
one_liner: A $16.6 billion speciality trades industry (2024) hit by acute labor shortages and tariff-driven material costs, now rebounding on residential demand and commercial infrastructure bids.
overview: Building finishing contractors—waterproofing, sheet metal, specialty fixtures, bath refinishing—serve both residential renovations and commercial/industrial construction. The industry has swung from pandemic-era ups to inflation pressures and is now stabilizing in 2025–2026 as interest rate relief spurs housing activity. But structural headwinds persist: 92% of construction firms struggle to hire skilled trades, materials like copper and steel are up 25–50% year-over-year (2025), and tariffs are pushing construction input prices up 8–12.6% annualized as of early 2026. The next wave of work is being captured by consolidators and larger players using AI/prefab to offset labor scarcity.

key_stats.growth: 0.6% in 2024; +3.6% CAGR past 5 years; projected moderate growth 2025–2029
key_stats.concentration: Low; dominated by small operators; private equity actively consolidating
key_stats.profit_margin: 6.7% (2022); margin pressure from labor costs and materials

current_dynamics: The industry is caught between two opposing forces. On one hand, interest rate cuts through 2025 and into 2026 are expected to unlock residential construction—the largest market segment (37% of revenue)—and boost home improvement spending. On the other hand, labor availability is structural: the average construction worker is 42.5 years old, only 16% of the workforce is under 35, and the industry needs 439,000 new workers just to meet 2025 demand. Compounding this, tariffs on imported steel and aluminum hit 50% on many products in 2025, driving metal prices up 25–50% for copper and 15–35% for steel; nonresidential construction input prices rose 12.6% annualized in early 2026, the fastest pace since 2022 supply-chain chaos. This has squeezed margins for small operators who can't absorb cost volatility. Meanwhile, consolidation is accelerating—private equity and larger contractors are acquiring smaller specialty shops to lock in labor capacity and achieve scale. Prefabrication and modular methods are being deployed to cut on-site worker dependence by 30–50%, and AI-driven project controls are beginning to reshape job-site productivity.
one_sentence: Finishing contractors face a structural labor crisis and tariff-driven input cost shock, creating margin pressure on small firms while larger, digitally-equipped consolidators capture market share.
whats_growing: Residential construction and home improvement spending (driven by falling mortgage rates). Prefabrication and modular systems (labor arbitrage). Commercial/industrial finishing tied to data centers and energy infrastructure (high-growth end markets). Consolidation and PE-backed platforms targeting specialty trades. Adoption of AI, robotics, and digital project management tools (up 37% of firms by 2025).
whats_shrinking: Traditional on-site labor-intensive methods. Small independent contractors (being acquired or pushed out). Price-competitive general contracting (tightening margins). Demand for secondary finishes in weak residential markets during rate-rise cycles.
themes: Energy code compliance and green building
Bidding shifts toward scale and technology
major_players: Consolidated platforms (private equity-backed groups; names not disclosed in sources but consolidation is accelerating)
Specialty electrical, HVAC, concrete contractors (drawing premium M&A valuations, 2025)
Smaller independent finishing shops (increasingly absorbed by larger firms)
Data center and infrastructure-focused finishing teams (high-growth captures)
recent_developments: August 2024: US market estimated at $16.6 billion; interest rate cuts flagged as primary growth catalyst through 2029.
2024–2025: Specialty contractor M&A volume jumped 38.6% YoY, driven by labor shortage concerns; subcontractor deals hit 366 transactions in 2025 vs 264 in 2024.
November 2025: Metal molding and trim prices surged ~50% YoY; copper tariff exposure pushes 2026 forecasts to +25–50% increases.
Early 2026: Nonresidential construction input prices rose 12.6% annualized (fastest since early 2022). Aggregate construction costs estimated to rise ~8% under tariff conditions.
2025–2026: 92% of construction firms report difficulty hiring qualified hourly craft workers; industry needs 439K net new workers in 2025, 349K in 2026, 456K in 2027.
January 2026: California 2025 Energy Code takes effect, raising insulation, ventilation, and heat-pump/electric-readiness baselines for all new residential and commercial permits.
outlook: The next 12–18 months will see growing divergence between large, well-capitalized consolidators and struggling small shops. Residential demand is poised to accelerate as mortgage rates ease further, but job-site productivity gains from prefab and automation will offset volume gains in employment. Tariff volatility and material-cost shock will persist into 2026–2027, keeping pressure on margins unless firms can raise prices—difficult in competitive/price-sensitive markets. Energy code tightening (California 2025 now in effect, others following) will force rework and retooling, favoring firms with digital project controls. PE investors will remain active, hunting for bolt-on acquisitions of specialty trades with "sticky" labor bases. Wage pressure will intensify as shortages bite harder, and firms that automate fastest will pull away from those staffed traditionally.

baseline_2022.growth: –0.1% CAGR 2017–2022 (includes pandemic dip); –0.7% decline in 2022 alone

title: US Frozen Fruit & Juice Production
one_liner: A $5.4 billion market split between declining frozen juice concentrates and surging frozen berries, upended by Coca-Cola's 80-year freeze on frozen orange juice.
overview: The US frozen fruit and juice production industry faces a sharp bifurcation in 2025-2026. Frozen berries and tropical fruits are booming—driven by smoothie culture, acai bowls, and health consciousness—but frozen juice concentrates are in free fall. Minute Maid's February 2026 discontinuation of its iconic 80-year frozen juice line marks the industry's largest symbolic rupture, as consumers moved to ready-to-drink and fresh juice years ago. Imports account for roughly 22% of domestic demand, with tariff relief in late 2025 benefiting Latin American suppliers. Frozen berries now represent over 55% of total frozen fruit consumption, while organic frozen fruit has captured nearly 40% of market value—commanding premiums as consumers trade up.

key_stats.growth: 0.1% annual growth in 2025; projected 1-1.5% CAGR through 2030
key_stats.profit_margin: 2.3-2.4% EBIT margin; expected to recover to 3.8% by 2026
key_stats.concentration: Low—fragmented with large players (Fresh Del Monte, Dole, General Mills) holding 25-30% combined, balanced by niche organic/premium entrants

current_dynamics: The industry has cleaved into two parallel markets with opposite trajectories. Frozen berries—strawberries (44.7% of 2025 US revenue), blueberries, raspberries, and mixed varieties—are riding health consciousness, convenience, and the smoothie-bowl phenomenon; the sector projects 11.5% CAGR through 2032. Meanwhile, frozen juice concentrates (26% of revenue in 2021, now lower) have collapsed as consumers switched to ready-to-drink and fresh juice starting in the early 2010s; Minute Maid's Q1 2026 discontinuation removes the industry's last cultural anchor. Imports—primarily from Canada, Mexico, Peru, and Chile—surged after November 2025 tariff exemptions removed duties on over 200 fruit preparations, lowering landed costs for downstream makers. Rising fruit input prices and labor costs (particularly in harvesting) are squeezing margins, while e-commerce and private-label penetration have democratized access, expanding retail shelf space for frozen fruit.
one_sentence: The industry is splitting apart: frozen berries booming at 11% CAGR on smoothie culture and health premiums, while frozen juice concentrates—capped by Minute Maid's end—crater to near-irrelevance.
whats_growing: Frozen berries (strawberries, blueberries, raspberries, mixed), tropical fruits, organic and premium single-variety packs, IQF (individually quick-frozen) technology-driven innovation, smoothie-bowl and functional-drink applications, acai puree (46% of acai market in 2025), private-label and e-commerce distribution, plant-based and superfood positioning.
whats_shrinking: Frozen juice concentrates (especially frozen orange juice concentrate), canned frozen juice products (Minute Maid discontinuation Q1 2026), traditional home-mixer juice applications, powder mixes and old-school concentrate thawing culture.
recent_developments: February 2026: Coca-Cola discontinues Minute Maid frozen juice concentrate after 80 years, phasing out iconic canned products in Q1 2026 due to 'shifting consumer preferences' toward ready-to-drink and fresh formats.

November 2025: US tariff exemptions remove duties on over 200 fruit preparations and juices, including orange juice and frozen fruit concentrates; benefits Latin American suppliers (Ecuador, Guatemala, El Salvador, Argentina).
September 2025: Greenyard acquisition via public-to-private deal led by Solum Partners and the Deprez family, signaling continued consolidation in packaged produce.

Q4 2025: Frozen fruit sector M&A activity accelerated with $51B invested in Q4 2025 alone over 20 quarters (Q1 2021-Q4 2025); Strategics lead in 'better-for-you' frozen acquisitions (24 BFY transactions YTD 2024-2025).

2025 Trend: Organic frozen fruit captures 39.7% of market value, with 28% YoY sales growth; acai puree dominates at 46% of acai segment; smoothie bowls via delivery grow 8% → 23% of urban consumption (2023-2026).

2025 Challenge: Brazil orange juice tariffs (existing + proposed 10%) could raise annual costs by $100M+ for US importers reliant on frozen concentrate; labor shortages in Canadian harvesting delay processing volumes.
current_competitive_landscape: Fresh Del Monte, Dole (market share fell from 25.5% in 2024 to 7.9% by 2026), General Mills, Agrana, Ardo, Greenyard (post-acquisition), Driscoll's (fresh berries, sourcing), Welch's (organic berries), and SunOpta (organic/non-GMO). Private-label brands via e-commerce (Amazon Fresh, Instacart) are fragmenting category share. Niche entrants (Blackbird Foods acquired by Ahimsa 2025, Blue Pacific Flavors acquired by Capol 2025) drive premiumization and plant-based innovation. The market remains low-concentration; no single player exceeds 15-20% share.
themes: Health & premiumization: organic/superfood/functional positioning captures 39.7% value share; acai, berries lead.
Death of juice concentrate: Minute Maid discontinuation marks cultural pivot from home-mixer to RTD; frozen OJ concentrate <7% of orange juice market by 2025.
Tariff volatility: November 2025 exemptions + Brazil tariff threats create cost swings; landed-cost unpredictability for importers.
E-commerce/private-label disruption: Shelf democratization via online channels erodes major-brand margins; niche organic brands gain share.
Supply-chain labor intensity: Harvest labor shortages (Canada, US) and rising fruit input costs squeeze 2.3% EBIT margins; automation accelerating.

Acai/smoothie-bowl culture: Frozen acai puree (46% of acai segment) and smoothie bowls ($507.6M market, 42.3% share) drive tropical/berry demand northward; delivery penetration at 23% in urban North America by 2026.
outlook: The industry will grow at a modest 1-1.5% CAGR to 2030, but composition will shift radically. Frozen berries and tropical fruits project 5-7% growth; frozen juice concentrates will approach zero or low single digits. Tariff relief and import competition from Latin America will keep pricing pressure on commodity segments, while premiumization (organic, acai, single-serve IQF, superfood blends) will grow at 7-10%+ CAGR. Consolidation will likely accelerate among mid-tier players unable to compete on price or scale; niche/organic entrants will fragment market further. Labor and input-cost inflation remain headwinds; automation investment will continue but labor scarcity (harvesting, processing) will remain tight through 2026-2027. The closure of Minute Maid and the shift to RTD/fresh juice are structural, not cyclical—frozen concentrates will remain a declining category.
